finding: The live range of $90-$750 is about right, but it is wide because it joins two different jobs: a cleaning (roughly $70-$230) and a replacement (roughly $140-$705 on the vehicles checked). Showing them as two ranges would be clearer. Built replacement totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2020 Jeep Compass 2.4L, $246.99-$545.00 + 0.6-1.0 hr = about $319-$705; midsize 2018 Chevrolet Malibu 1.5L, $114.40-$233.38 + 0.2-1.0 hr = about $138-$393; truck 2016 Ford F-150 5.0L, $139.49-$400.73 + 0.5-1.0 hr = about $199-$561; luxury 2016 Lincoln MKZ Hybrid 2.0L, $171.72-$278.18 + 0.5-1.0 hr = about $232-$438. Cautions on the low ends: the Malibu and MKZ lows are the genuine part at an online discount price, not an aftermarket part (for the Malibu none could be priced; for the MKZ the one aftermarket price found, a Dorman unit, is printed without a decimal point and is kept only as a cross-check at an implied $161.99), and the F-150 low is a budget-brand aftermarket unit; with a name-brand or dealer part and a normal shop time, most replacements land between about $300 and $700. Changes on the second look (2026-11-20): (1) the luxury example was switched from the 2011 Cadillac CTS to the 2016 Lincoln MKZ Hybrid, because the only stated CTS time (GM 0.8 hr) includes diagnosis and the relearn and so is a larger job, while Ford prints a plain 'Replace ETB' time of 0.5 hr for the 2016 MKZ and names the same throttle body part number the catalog lists for the hybrid. This lowers the luxury range from about $288-$517 to about $232-$438; the all-classes span ($138-$705) is unchanged. (2) The Malibu high end was the older Malibu's 0.8 hr, which also includes diagnosis; it is now a cross-check and the high end is the general 1.0 hr used in the other classes, which raises the Malibu top from about $361 to about $393. (3) The 2016 F-150 time (0.5 hr) turns out to be for a truck whose only listed part is a V6 throttle body, so it is most likely not the 5.0L; the same 0.5 hr is printed for the 2018 F-150 5.0L, which is now the stated low, and the number did not change. The 2018-2020 5.0L genuine part lists at $545.82, so that truck builds to about $706 at the top. Cleaning only: a mechanic-written consumer guide (Jerry) gives 0.5-0.8 hr for a typical cleaning and 0.8-1.2 hr when the throttle body is removed for a deep clean, which is $60-$192 of labor at $120-$160/hr, plus about $10-$40 for cleaner and a gasket: roughly $70-$230. A relearn with a scan tool adds 0.2-0.4 hr ($24-$64) per the same guide; an Acura bulletin prints 0.2 hr for 'Reset the throttle position value and idle learn procedure'. One GM bulletin allows 1.2 hr for remove, clean, replace the sensor cover, relearn and diagnosis together. So the $90 floor fits a cleaning (lowest benchmark $90), and nothing found supports a replacement that cheap except the Malibu built on a discounted part and a 0.2 hr warranty time. The $750 top fits the mainstream cases but can be exceeded: RepairPal's average is $623-$766, YourMechanic shows $807-$1,204 at a shop or dealer for a 2017 F-150 3.5L turbo, the 2.0L turbo MKZ throttle body lists at $543.64 against $278.18 for the hybrid, and a 2024-2025 Jeep Wrangler 2.0L turbo bulletin allows 2.7 hr for the throttle body alone ($324-$432 of labor before parts). How solid the labor times are: three of the four low ends are manufacturer warranty times stated for the example vehicle (Compass 0.6 hr, which is an 'inspect and replace' operation; Malibu 0.2 hr; MKZ 0.5 hr), and the truck low is the same engine two model years later (2018 F-150 5.0L, 0.5 hr). Other maker times seen sit in the same band: 0.5 hr Ford Fusion, 0.6 hr Lincoln MKT, Ford Edge/Taurus and a 2021 Colorado diesel (diagnosis billed separately). These are warranty times, the low end of what shops bill; the Malibu's 0.2 hr sits beside charge-air-tube work and looks optimistic as a stand-alone job. Every high end is the same general figure, a consumer guide's 50-60 minutes of billed labor, not a time for the example vehicle; a parts seller's do-it-yourself estimate of about 2 hours for an older F-150 5.0L suggests the 1.0 hr top can be exceeded. Only three of the eight hour figures are for the example vehicle, which is why confidence stays low. Parts: every class has two priced sources, but two lows are discounted genuine parts rather than aftermarket, the Compass aftermarket price is a 'from' price on a 2019 listing, and the luxury example is a domestic hybrid sedan; no European luxury throttle body was priced and no stated time for one was found, and those can cost more. Our totals sit below RepairPal mainly because its parts figure ($492-$573) is higher than the list prices found for the Malibu, the 2016 F-150 and the MKZ. An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis or scan fee, a new throttle body gasket (about $18 list on the Compass), shop supplies and tax. Many shops try a cleaning first: about 0.5-1.2 hr of labor plus cleaner, roughly $70-$230. After either a cleaning or a replacement, most drive-by-wire cars need an idle/throttle relearn, which some shops include and others bill at about 0.2-0.4 hr. An air filter, intake tube or clamp, or a wiring connector repair may be quoted at the same time. An estimate is not a quote and not a diagnosis: the same warning light or reduced-power message can come from wiring, the pedal sensor or a vacuum leak.
